name: al-Mumazzaq
bio: Sha's ibn Nahar, called al-Mumazzaq, was the sister's son of al-Muthaqqib and, like him, of the Lukaiz division of 'Abd al-Qais. Lyall says very little of his work has survived.
In Ode LXXXI he mentions an-Nu'man Abu Qabus, the last king of al-Hirah.

poems.author: al-Mumazzaq
poems.note: Lyall's heading: Sha's son of Nahar, of Nukrah, of Lukaiz, of 'Abd al-Qais, called al-Mumazzaq. Lyall appends a second version of this poem, as ascribed to Yazid ibn al-Khadhdhaq; that version is not reproduced here.

poems.title: Ode LXXXI: The heart that was smitten with
poems.author: al-Mumazzaq
poems.text:
The heart that was smitten with longing is sobered of its youthful passion, and the time has come for the scattering of the whole tribe collected together ;

Then was he as though not the showers that fall from the clouds, nor the far-sought wine strained from the lees could cure the burning thirst of his heart.

Now who will carry to an-Nu'man this message, that his sister's son repairs constantly to as-Safa above the 'Ain, and sings ;

And that Lukaiz are not the owners of a skinful of clarified butter, what time their pilgrims rose high [to the Upland] and dispersed to their several lands ?

[God (?)] decreed for the whole of the men, when his commandment came to them, that they should lead their horses alongside [of their camels] and then should overtake their foes.

A generous, noble chief makes with them for the rugged Upland — one keen and swift to strike like the edge of an Indian blade.

And the whole concourse said — ' Whither tends our way ? ' and Mumazzaq hid within from them the evil guile of his mind.

And when the [fields of the] rimth and the ghada covered them from view, and when the fires of both the parties shone before them,

And he [the leader (?)] diverted them westwards away from our country— and those about us had been glad if he had gone eastwards
